Huai Bong Dairy Farm Opens Applications for the
2027 Young Cheesemaker Fellowship
Huai Bong Dairy Farm Co., Ltd. · Press release Ref. HB-PR-2026-09 · For immediate release · 21 September
2026
DAN KHUN THOT, Nakhon Ratchasima, 21 September 2026 – Huai Bong Dairy Farm today
announced the third intake of the Huai Bong Young Cheesemaker Fellowship, a 14-week programme that
teaches young smallholder dairy farmers to turn part of their own milk into fresh and short-aged cheese
and sell it locally. The 2027 cohort will have 12 places, up from 8 places in each of the 2025 and 2026
cohorts, and the monthly stipend rises to 6,500 baht. Until the 2026 cohort the stipend was 5,000 baht
per month.
"Most small farms in our area sell every litre to the collection centre at the same price, whatever the
season," said Orathai Sukpracha, Managing Director of Huai Bong Dairy Farm. "We want young farmers
to keep their herds, not sell them."
1. Programme dates and structure
The 2027 fellowship runs from Monday 11 January 2027 to Friday 16 April 2027 in three phases:
Phase 1, weeks 1–6 (11 January to 19 February): full-time training in the Huai Bong creamery,
Building 4, Monday to Friday from 07:30 to 16:00. Topics include milk hygiene, starter cultures,
pressing and labelling.
Phase 2, weeks 7–12 (22 February to 2 April): fellows make cheese on their own farms. A mentor
from the Huai Bong creamery visits each fellow every second Thursday.
Phase 3, weeks 13–14 (5 to 16 April): final assessment of each fellow's cheese and a public Market
Day at the Huai Bong farm shop on Saturday 10 April 2027, where every fellow runs a stall.
Accommodation in the farm dormitory and three meals a day are provided free of charge during Phase 1
only.
2. Who can apply
Applicants must meet all of the following conditions:
Aged 20 to 35 on 1 January 2027.
Currently milking at least 5 and no more than 40 cows on a farm they run themselves or with their
family.
Delivering milk to a collection centre in Nakhon Ratchasima, Chaiyaphum or Buriram province.
Able to attend all of Phase 1 in person.
Age exception. Applicants aged 36 to 40 on 1 January 2027 may also apply if they took over the
day-to-day running of a family dairy farm on or after 1 January 2025. They must attach a letter from
the village headman or the collection centre confirming the handover date. Former fellows of the
2025 or 2026 cohorts cannot apply again.

3. What fellows receive
Stipend: 6,500 baht per month for the four months from January to April 2027, paid by bank transfer
on the last working day of each month.
Starter kit: equipment worth about 38,000 baht, including a 50-litre stainless steel vat with heater, a
screw cheese press, 20 moulds, a digital probe thermometer and a pH meter.
Certificate: fellows who pass the final assessment receive the Huai Bong Cheesemaker Certificate at
the Market Day.
Fellows keep all income from the cheese they make and sell during Phases 2 and 3. Huai Bong does not
take a share and does not buy fellows' cheese.
4. Commitments and conditions
Fellows must attend at least 90 % of Phase 1 training days, which is 27 of the 30 days. A fellow who
misses more than 3 days in Phase 1 without a medical certificate leaves the programme. In Phase 2,
fellows must send a short weekly production log to their mentor by Sunday evening; the stipend for a
month is withheld if two or more logs from that month are missing.
The starter kit becomes the fellow's property on successful completion of the programme. A fellow who
leaves the programme for any reason before the end of week 12 must return the kit within 14 days. A
fellow who leaves during Phase 3 keeps the kit but does not receive the certificate.
5. How to apply
1. Complete the application form online on the Huai Bong website or on paper at the farm office in
Building 2, open Monday to Saturday from 08:00 to 17:00.
2. Attach a copy of your national ID card, your farm registration document, milk delivery slips for the last
3 months, and a one-page letter explaining what cheese you want to make and why.
3. Submit by 17:00 on Sunday 15 November 2026. Applications open on 1 October 2026; late
applications are not accepted.
Shortlisted applicants are interviewed at the farm from 1 to 4 December 2026, and the final shortlist
includes a visit to the applicant's own farm. Results are announced by telephone and on the website on
11 December 2026.
About Huai Bong Dairy Farm
Huai Bong Dairy Farm is a family-owned dairy farm in Dan Khun Thot district, Nakhon Ratchasima,
founded in 1998. Its on-farm creamery opened in 2019. The Young Cheesemaker Fellowship started in
2025 and has trained 16 fellows from three provinces so far.

telephone 044 389 217, email press@huaibongdairy.example.

Mekkala Mobile Launches TideLine Fleet Plan for
Small Fishing Boats
Mekkala Telecom Public Company Limited · Press Release MK-PR-2026-031 · Issued 28 September 2026 ·
For immediate release
SONGKHLA, 28 September 2026 – Mekkala Telecom Public Company Limited (Mekkala Mobile) today
announced the TideLine Fleet Plan, a mobile service designed for small-scale fishing boats working
along the lower Gulf coast between Pattani and Nakhon Si Thammarat. The plan goes on sale on 15
October 2026 and uses nine new high-mast coastal sites that extend usable voice and data coverage to
about 40 kilometres offshore in normal weather. Before these sites were switched on, Mekkala's
coverage along this coast ended about 12 kilometres from shore, while most family boats fish 15 to 35
kilometres out.
"Fishing families asked for a way to call for help, early storm warnings and a simple way to say they are
safe. TideLine puts all three on an ordinary phone," said Phanida Thongsuk, Head of Coastal Networks at
Mekkala Mobile.
1. What the TideLine Fleet Plan includes
Monthly price: 199 baht per boat, including VAT. This covers the captain's main SIM. During the pilot
the price was 149 baht; the pilot price ends on 14 October 2026 and all pilot boats move to the
standard price from the November 2026 bill.
Data and calls: 20 GB of mobile data per month, unlimited calls between phones registered on
TideLine plans, and 100 minutes per month to other Thai mobile and landline numbers.
SeaCall distress code *4848: dialling *4848 connects directly to the Mekkala Maritime Watch Room
in Hat Yai, which is staffed 24 hours a day. The call is free and works even when the SIM has no
remaining balance. Its staff pass the boat's last known position to coast rescue volunteers.
Storm alerts: warning SMS messages are sent in Thai, English and Burmese whenever forecast wind
for the boat's registered fishing zone reaches Beaufort force 6 or higher.
Safe check-in: the captain sends the word POS by SMS to 4848. If a boat that has started a trip
sends no check-in for 12 hours, the Watch Room calls the boat first and then the registered shore
contact.
2. Coverage area
The nine new sites stand at Sai Buri (Pattani), Thepha, Chana, Singhanakhon, Sathing Phra and Ranot
(Songkhla), and Hua Sai, Pak Phanang and Sichon (Nakhon Si Thammarat). Coverage at 40 kilometres
requires the external boat antenna described in section 4; a handset used on deck without it normally
keeps a signal to about 25 kilometres.
Note. Coverage around Ko Kra and in the open water east of it is not part of the TideLine service
area. Boats fishing there should continue to carry radio equipment. SeaCall *4848 still works
wherever any Mekkala signal is available.

3. Who can join
The plan is open to boats under 30 gross tons that hold a valid provincial fishing licence and are based at
a pier in Pattani, Songkhla or Nakhon Si Thammarat. The boat owner must be resident in Thailand and
register the plan in his or her own name. Trawlers of 30 gross tons and above use Mekkala's business
fleet contracts instead.
Each boat can add up to five crew SIMs in addition to the captain's main SIM, so a boat can have at
most six TideLine SIMs. Each crew SIM costs 99 baht per month and receives 5 GB of data, unlimited
calls to other TideLine phones, and the same SeaCall and storm alert services as the main SIM. Crew
members who are not Thai nationals can receive a crew SIM by showing a valid passport or work permit.
4. How to register
1. The boat owner brings the boat registration book, the fishing licence and his or her ID card to any
Mekkala shop in the three provinces, or to the TideLine service van, which visits the main fishing
piers every Saturday from 08:00 to 14:00.
2. The owner names one shore contact, whose phone number must not belong to anyone who sails on
the same boat.
3. The owner chooses the boat's fishing zone on a printed map, so storm alerts match the area where
the boat actually works. The zone can be changed later at a shop or through the Maritime Services
Desk.
4. A Mekkala technician fits the external boat antenna at the pier. The antenna normally costs 1,200
baht but is fitted free for boats registered by 31 December 2026.
5. Before the boat leaves the pier, the captain makes a test call to *4848 and the Watch Room confirms
the boat's name and shore contact. The plan is active within 24 hours of a successful test call.
5. Results of the Chana pilot
From 2 March to 31 August 2026, 214 boats from Chana and Thepha tested the service. The Watch
Room handled 3 genuine distress calls, alerting rescue volunteers in an average of 7 minutes. Storm
alerts reached 96 per cent of registered phones before crews left the pier.
6. Support and responsibilities
Network building and the coastal site programme are led by Phanida Thongsuk, Head of Coastal
Networks. Day-to-day customer matters for the plan, including registration problems, missing storm
alerts, changes to the shore contact and complaints about coverage at sea, are handled by the Maritime
Services Desk, managed by Ekachai Boonma. The desk can be reached on 0 7430 4848 from 07:00 to
21:00 every day, or through the "TideLine" menu in the Mekkala app. Emergencies at sea must always go
to SeaCall *4848, not to the desk number.
About Mekkala Mobile. Mekkala Telecom Public Company Limited was founded in 2009 and has its
head office in Hat Yai, Songkhla. It serves about 3.1 million mobile customers in southern Thailand.
Media contact: Ratchanee Siriphan, Corporate Communications, Mekkala Telecom Public Company
Limited, telephone 0 7430 1100, email press@mekkala-mobile.example.

Incident Report: Duplicate PlanAhead Scheduled
Payments in the RimPay App on 25 September 2026
Rimping Thrift Bank Public Company Limited, Digital Channels Division, Chiang Mai · Ref. RTB-INC-2026-031
· Version 2.0 · Issued 1 October 2026
1. Summary
On the morning of Friday 25 September 2026, the monthly salary day for most of our customers, the
PlanAhead feature of the RimPay mobile banking app executed a large number of scheduled transfers
and bill payments twice. The duplicate debits were taken between 06:00 and 08:42, when the Digital
Incident Manager, Sirinya Phromwong, paused all PlanAhead processing. Normal processing resumed at
13:15 the same day after a corrected scheduler had been tested.
No customer data was exposed and no money left the bank's control without a matching instruction from
the customer. The problem was that one valid instruction was carried out twice. Every affected customer
has now been refunded the duplicated amount in full, together with any fees and interest that the
duplicate caused. Section 5 explains how customers can claim other costs, such as late-payment
charges from another company.
Version 1.0 of this report was issued on 27 September; this version 2.0 adds the final refund figures and
the corrected claim deadline.
2. Timeline
24 September, 22:30 – The PlanAhead scheduler is upgraded from version 4.1 to version 4.2 during
a planned maintenance window. Post-release checks pass.
25 September, 05:58 – A network fault interrupts the link between the primary data centre in Mae
Rim and the secondary data centre in Lamphun for about 40 seconds.
06:00 – The daily PlanAhead run starts. Both data centres begin processing the same batch of
scheduled instructions.
06:47 – The first customer call about a double salary transfer to a family member reaches the RimPay
call centre.
07:35 – Call volume reaches four times the normal level. The duty supervisor opens an incident with
the Digital Operations team.
08:42 – Sirinya Phromwong pauses all PlanAhead processing. Instructions due later that day are
held.
09:30 – An in-app banner and a push notification tell customers that some scheduled payments were
taken twice and will be corrected.
11:10 – The cause is confirmed and the scheduler is rolled back to version 4.1.
13:15 – PlanAhead processing resumes. The held instructions are executed once each by 14:05.

3. Cause
Version 4.2 of the scheduler moved the check that prevents an instruction from running twice from the
shared database into each data centre's local memory. When the network link failed at 05:58, the
secondary data centre in Lamphun believed that the primary site was down and took over the daily run.
The primary site in Mae Rim was in fact still working and also ran the batch. Because each site kept its
own record of which instructions it had completed, neither site could see that the other had already paid
them.
The test plan for version 4.2 did not include a network split between the two data centres during a live
run. The release also went ahead the night before salary day, which the bank's change calendar marks as
a "caution" date but did not at that time block.
Note. Instructions created with the "Pay now" button, card payments and QR payments at shops do
not use the PlanAhead scheduler and were not affected. Recurring loan repayments collected by the
bank itself also run on a separate system and were taken once only.
4. Customer impact and refunds
4.1 Scale
On 25 September, 18,412 PlanAhead instructions were due for execution. Of these, 6,935 instructions
were executed twice, belonging to 5,208 customers. The duplicated payments totalled 41.7 million baht.
The largest single duplicate was a scheduled rent transfer of 186,000 baht; the median duplicate was
3,500 baht.
The duplicates fell into two groups:
Payments to accounts at Rimping Thrift Bank: 4,102 duplicates. These were reversed
automatically from the receiving accounts and returned to the customers by 14:00 on 25 September.
Payments to other banks and to billers: 2,833 duplicates. These could not be reversed directly and
had to be recalled through each receiving bank or biller. By 29 September, 2,391 of them had been
returned. The bank is still pursuing the rest.
To avoid customers waiting for the remaining recalls, the bank credited every customer with an
unreturned interbank or biller duplicate in full on 30 September. Any money recovered from the receiving
side after that date is kept by the bank and is not taken again from the customer.
4.2 Fees and interest refunded automatically
Customers do not need to apply for the following. They were credited on 30 September and appear in
the statement with the description "RTB-INC-031 REFUND":
Interbank transfer fee: the 15-baht fee charged for each duplicate transfer to another bank.
FlexLine overdraft interest: all interest charged on FlexLine overdraft balances between 25 and 30
September, whether or not the overdraft was caused by the duplicate.
Returned item fee: the 50-baht fee for any other debit that failed for insufficient funds on 25 or 26
September.

From 1 August 2026 the returned item fee is 50 baht; before that date it was 80 baht. Because the
incident happened after 1 August, refunds are made at the 50-baht rate.
Note. Biller late-payment charges are not refunded automatically, because the bank cannot see
them. They are covered by the claim process in Section 5.
5. How to claim other costs
Customers who had other costs because of a duplicate PlanAhead payment, for example a late charge
from a utility company or a bounced cheque fee at another bank, can claim them back. Claims must be
received by 31 October 2026. The first customer notice of 25 September gave a deadline of 15 October;
this has been extended.
1. In RimPay, open Help, then Report a problem, and choose the topic "25 September duplicate
payment".
2. Select the affected PlanAhead instruction from the list. Only instructions due on 25 September are
shown.
3. Enter the amount you are claiming and a short description of the cost.
4. Attach evidence, such as a bill showing the late charge or a statement from the other bank.
5. Submit the claim. You will receive a claim number starting with "DPC-" by push notification.
Customers who do not use RimPay for this purpose can make the same claim at any Rimping Thrift Bank
branch using form RT-CL7, bringing their ID card and the evidence.
Claims of up to 5,000 baht are decided by the Customer Care team within 10 business days. Claims
above 5,000 baht are referred to the Customer Care Review Panel, chaired by Wasan Thepsuriya, Head
of Customer Care, and are decided within 20 business days. Approved amounts are paid into the
account that the PlanAhead payment was made from.
6. Corrective actions
Duplicate guard (completed 27 September): the scheduler again checks the shared database

Minutes of the Service Credit Review Panel,
Meeting No. 4/2026
Lomfah Cloud Co., Ltd. · Ref. SCRP-04/2026 · Meeting held 24 September 2026 · Minutes approved 1
October 2026
Venue: Meeting Room 7B, Lomfah Cloud head office, Sathorn, Bangkok, with a video link to the Bang
Na operations centre, 14:00–16:10. Present: Orawan Thepsiri (Head of Customer Assurance, chair),
Kittipat Boonmee (Storage SRE Lead), Pimchanok Saelim (Billing Manager), Teerawat Inkaew (Legal
Counsel). Minutes: Sasiwimon Jaidee (Customer Assurance Officer). Apologies: Narong Sukprasert
(Head of Platform Operations).
1. Incident INC-2609-031: BlockVault degradation in zone BKK-2
Kittipat Boonmee presented the incident. On Saturday 12 September 2026, Lomfah BlockVault block
storage in zone BKK-2 (Bang Na) had very high write latency and timeouts from 09:42 to 13:17, a total of
3 hours 35 minutes. The root cause was a firmware update (version 7.4.1) installed on two storage
controller pairs during a maintenance window that should have covered only one pair. Service recovered
after the firmware was rolled back to version 7.3.8. Zone BKK-1 (Lat Krabang) and the Chiang Mai zone
CNX-1 were not affected.
Affected customer accounts: 418, with 1,926 volumes on the two controller pairs.
Measured monthly uptime of affected BlockVault volumes for September 2026: 99.50 %.
The public post-incident report was published on the status page on 19 September 2026.
2. Credit level for INC-2609-031
Under the Lomfah Cloud Service Level Agreement version 3.2, monthly uptime below 99.95 % gives a
credit of 10 % of the monthly charge for the affected service, below 99.0 % gives 25 %, and below 95.0
% gives 50 %. With 99.50 % uptime, the standard credit for this incident is therefore 10 %.
Decision 4/2026-1. Because the outage was caused by a Lomfah change-control error and not by
hardware failure, the panel agreed a goodwill uplift: customers on the Business or Enterprise support
plan receive 15 % of their September 2026 BlockVault charge in BKK-2. Customers on the Starter plan
receive the standard 10 %.
3. Claims: deadline and procedure
SLA version 3.2 has applied since 1 July 2026. Until 30 June 2026 (SLA version 3.1), a claim had to be
filed within 14 days of the incident. Under version 3.2, a claim must be filed within 30 days after the end
of the month in which the incident happened. For INC-2609-031 the panel confirmed that claims must
be received by 31 October 2026. The procedure agreed for customers is:
1. Sign in to the Lomfah console with an account owner or billing administrator role.
2. Open Support, then Billing, then “Service credit claim”, and quote incident number INC-2609-031.
3. List the affected volume IDs, or tick “all BlockVault volumes in BKK-2”.

4. Billing confirms the credit amount by email within 10 working days of the claim.
Credits are not paid in cash. They are applied to the next invoice and expire 12 months after they are
issued. Credits for one month can never exceed 50 % of the monthly charge for the affected service.
Note on unpaid invoices. SLA version 3.2 normally refuses credits to an account with an unpaid
invoice more than 60 days overdue. For INC-2609-031 only, the panel agreed (Decision 4/2026-2) to
accept the claim if every overdue invoice is fully paid by 31 October 2026, the same day as the claim
deadline.
4. Escalated individual claims
Account LC-77214 (online retailer, Hat Yai, Business plan) asked for 50 % of its whole September bill
because of lost sales. The panel declined: the SLA excludes lost revenue and other indirect losses.
The account receives 15 % of its BKK-2 BlockVault charge, in line with Decision 4/2026-1.
Account LC-80533 (university research group, Starter plan) claimed for slow storage on 12
September. All its volumes are in BKK-1, which was not affected, so the claim was rejected. Kittipat
Boonmee will check the latency logs for that day and reply to the customer directly.
5. Change process review and SLA version 3.3
Narong Sukprasert sent a written update: from 1 October 2026 every BlockVault firmware change needs
a second approver from a different team, and changes may cover only one controller pair per
maintenance window. The panel then discussed the draft of SLA version 3.3, planned to take effect on 1
January 2027. The main proposals are:
Automatic credits, with no claim needed, for any incident that affects more than 100 customer
accounts.
A longer claim period for all other incidents: 60 days after the end of the incident month instead of
30.
The credit tiers of 10 %, 25 % and 50 % stay the same.
Customers must be told about SLA changes at least 60 days before they take effect, so the customer
notice has to go out by 2 November 2026. Teerawat Inkaew will deliver the final legal text of version 3.3
by 23 October 2026.
6. Action points
Email all 418 affected accounts with the credit level and claim steps by 26 September 2026:
Sasiwimon Jaidee.
Set up the 15 % and 10 % credit codes in the billing system by 30 September 2026: Pimchanok
Saelim.
Reply to account LC-80533 after the latency log check by 2 October 2026: Kittipat Boonmee.
Final legal text of SLA version 3.3 by 23 October 2026: Teerawat Inkaew.
Next meeting: Thursday 5 November 2026, 14:00, Meeting Room 7B, after the claim deadline has
passed.

Internal Memo: Closure of the Basement Stores
and New River Level Stages
Sawan Wari Heritage Archive, Nakhon Sawan · Ref. ADM-MEMO-2026-31 · 14 October 2026
To: All staff, volunteers and reading room attendants
From: Kanokwan Srisuk, Director (Room 2-01, ext. 201)
Copy: Duangporn Chaiyasit, Head of Collections; Thawatchai Inthara, Facilities and Flood Officer
Subject: Permanent closure of basement stores B1 and B2, relocation timetable and revised flood
stages, effective 1 November 2026
1. Background
On the night of 22 September 2026 river water entered basement store B2 through the cable duct under
the east loading bay. About 4 cm of water stood on the floor for six hours before the pump cleared it. No
boxes were wet because the lowest shelf in B2 is 15 cm above the floor, but 38 boxes of the Phayuha
Khiri land deed collection were moved upstairs in a hurry and 6 of them were damaged in handling. The
Board of Trustees reviewed the incident on 9 October 2026 and approved the decisions in this memo.
2. Decision
Basement stores B1 and B2 will no longer be used for any archival material. From 1 November 2026 no
new accessions may be placed in either room. All existing holdings will be moved to the new store on
level 3 (Room 3-10, the former staff training room), which has been fitted with mobile shelving for 2,400
standard boxes. The basement will only hold empty boxes, cleaning supplies and the spare pump.
The relocation runs in three phases:
Phase 1, 2 to 20 November 2026: B2 holdings, starting with the land deed collection and the
municipal maps.
Phase 2, 23 November to 18 December 2026: B1 holdings, starting with photographs and negatives.
Phase 3, 5 to 29 January 2027: oversize items and the newspaper bound volumes, which need the
hired stair lift.
The reading room stays open during Phases 1 and 2, but requests for items from B1 or B2 will be served
within 3 working days instead of the usual same day. During Phase 3 the reading room closes on
Mondays and Tuesdays so the stair lift can use the main corridor.
Note. The 6 damaged deed boxes are not part of the move. They stay in the conservation lab (Room
1-04) until the conservator from Chiang Mai has assessed them, expected in the week of 16
November 2026.
3. Revised river level stages
Our flood stages now use the reading on the archive's own gauge board at the Pier 2 steps, read twice a
day (08:00 and 16:00) by the security guard on duty and entered in the River Log. Until 31 October 2026

the stages were based on the provincial rainfall warnings, which proved too slow in September.
Stage 1, Watch: gauge at 2.80 m or more. Facilities checks the pump and the duct seals daily and
reads the gauge every 2 hours during opening hours.
Stage 2, Prepare: gauge at 3.40 m or more. Sandbags are placed at the east loading bay and the
basement door, and anything left in the basement is lifted onto pallets.
Stage 3, Protect: gauge at 3.90 m or more. The reading room closes to the public, the ground floor
exhibition cases are emptied to level 2, and the main electricity board for the basement is switched
off.
On 22 September the gauge reached 3.72 m, so under the new rules the archive would have been at
Stage 2 about 30 hours before the water came in.
4. Who declares a stage
Thawatchai Inthara declares Stages 1 and 2 and informs all staff by the LINE group "SWHA Duty". Only
the Director can declare Stage 3, or the Head of Collections if the Director cannot be reached within 1
hour. A stage is lowered only after the gauge has stayed below its threshold for 24 hours. Volunteers do
not move collection items at Stage 3; they help with sandbags and visitor information only.
5. What to do if you find water in a store
1. Do not switch on lights or equipment if water is touching any socket or cable. Leave the room and
call security on ext. 100.
2. Call Thawatchai Inthara on 081 552 4093 (24 hours). If he does not answer within 15 minutes, call the
Director.
3. Photograph the room and the water line before anything is moved, and note the time and the gauge
reading.
4. Move only boxes that are already wet or within 10 cm of the water, using the yellow crates kept
outside Room 1-04. Record every box number on the Emergency Move Sheet (form SWHA-F12).
5. Hand the sheet to the Head of Collections before the end of your shift. Wet paper must reach the
conservation lab within 48 hours so it can be frozen before mould starts.
6. Staff time and training
Each department lends 2 staff to the relocation team on Wednesdays and Thursdays during Phases 1
and 2. Overtime for weekend moving is paid at the archive's holiday rate of 1.5 times the normal hourly
rate, capped at 12 hours per person per month. All staff who will handle boxes must attend the 90-
minute safe lifting and box handling session in Room 2-05 on either 28 or 30 October 2026, starting at
13:30. Register with Duangporn Chaiyasit (ext. 214) by 24 October.
The updated Flood Readiness Plan, version 3.0, replaces version 2.2 and is in the shared folder under
Facilities. Questions on the move go to Duangporn Chaiyasit; questions on the stages and the River Log
go to Thawatchai Inthara (ext. 118).

Thale Khiao Reef Foundation Launches Starfish
Sweep 2026 to Contain Crown-of-Thorns Outbreak
off Koh Phangan
Thale Khiao Reef Foundation · Press release Ref. TKRF-PR-2026-09 · For immediate release · 21 September
2026
THONG SALA, KOH PHANGAN, 21 September 2026 — The Thale Khiao Reef Foundation today
announced Starfish Sweep 2026, a four-month campaign with local dive operators to remove crown-of-
thorns starfish from reefs around Koh Phangan and the Sail Rock pinnacle. The campaign runs from 1
October 2026 to 31 January 2027 and follows a Foundation survey that found outbreak-level numbers of
the coral-eating starfish at two of the three monitored sites.
1. What the September survey found
Foundation survey teams counted starfish along fixed transects at three sites between 2 and 6
September 2026. The Foundation treats a reef as being in outbreak when it holds more than 15 adult
starfish per hectare, the level at which the starfish eat coral faster than it can regrow.
Sail Rock: 38 starfish per hectare, the highest count recorded at the site since monitoring began in
2019. Live hard coral cover on the eastern wall fell from 46 % in March 2026 to 31 % in September.
Mae Haad and the Koh Ma channel: 22 starfish per hectare, up from 11 per hectare at the end of the
2025–26 pilot.
Chalok Baan Kao bay: 9 starfish per hectare, below the outbreak level. This site will be monitored but
not swept.
Feeding scars, which show as fresh white patches of dead coral, were seen on about one table coral in
four at Sail Rock. Divers also reported clusters of juvenile starfish shorter than 15 cm, which suggests
that a second wave of adults could appear in 2027 if nothing is done.
"Crown-of-thorns starfish are a natural part of the reef, but at these numbers they can strip a coral wall in
a single season," said Dr. Kanittha Sombatwong, Executive Director of the Thale Khiao Reef Foundation.
"The pilot at Mae Haad showed that trained local divers can bring numbers down quickly. This year we
are paying operators more, and we are going out to Sail Rock, where the damage is worst."
2. Results of the 2025–26 pilot
The Foundation ran a smaller pilot at Mae Haad only, from 12 November 2025 to 28 February 2026, with
four dive operators and its own staff divers. Over 61 diving days the pilot removed 3,140 starfish, and the
density at Mae Haad fell from 41 to 11 starfish per hectare. No diver was injured by a starfish spine
during the pilot, although two divers needed treatment for minor jellyfish stings. The pilot cost 512,000
baht, which was paid for entirely by the Foundation's own reserves.
Starfish Sweep 2026 sets a combined removal target of 9,000 starfish across Sail Rock and Mae Haad,
with the aim of bringing both sites below 10 starfish per hectare by the end of January 2027.

3. Who can take part
Any dive operator based on Koh Phangan or Koh Samui may join, provided it has a valid boat and
business licence and registers with the Foundation before its first sweep dive. Registration opens on 23
September 2026 and closes on 15 October 2026. Operators who join after the campaign has started may
begin sweeping on the Monday after their registration is confirmed.
Each diver who culls starfish must meet all of the following conditions:
hold an advanced open water certification or higher, from any recognised training agency;
have at least 30 logged dives, of which at least 10 were made in the Gulf of Thailand;
complete the Foundation's three-hour Starfish Sweep training session, which covers species
identification, the injection method, spine safety and data recording.
Training sessions are held in Training Room 2 of the Foundation's office on Thong Sala Pier Road,
starting at 09:00 on 28 September, 5 October and 12 October 2026. Each session takes up to 16 divers.
Divers who completed the pilot training in 2025 must attend a one-hour refresher instead, because the
injection method has changed (see section 4). Training is free of charge, and operators may send as
many divers as they wish.
4. How the starfish are removed
Divers remove the starfish in place, using a single injection from the Foundation's sealed injection kit. The
kit and the dose are set out in the Foundation's field protocol TK-COTS-3, which replaces the TK-COTS-
2 protocol used in the pilot. Under the old protocol each starfish received two injections; under TK-
COTS-3 one injection is enough, which roughly doubles the number of starfish a diver can treat on one
tank. Starfish are not brought to the surface, because handling them on the boat caused most of the
spine injuries recorded by other programmes.
Kits are issued to registered operators free of charge from the Foundation office and must be returned,
used or unused, by 7 February 2027. Each kit treats about 120 starfish. Operators who lose a kit are
charged 2,500 baht for its replacement.
Dive rules during the sweep
Sweep dives must be made in buddy pairs. Only one diver of each pair injects; the other records and
watches for hazards.
No culling deeper than 18 metres, even if the diver is certified to go deeper.
No sweep dive may start if underwater visibility is less than 5 metres or if the Foundation has posted
a strong-current warning for the site.
At Sail Rock, divers must not enter the vertical swim-through known as the Chimney during a sweep
dive. Starfish found there are reported for removal by Foundation staff.
Inside the roped coral nursery at Mae Haad, only Foundation staff divers may cull starfish. Operator
divers who see a starfish inside the nursery ropes report its position in the app and leave it in place.
Note. Every sweep dive must be logged in the ReefTally app within 24 hours of surfacing, with the
site, the GPS mark, the maximum depth, the number of starfish treated and at least one photo per
ten starfish. Dives logged after 24 hours are recorded for science but are not paid.

5. Payments to dive operators
The Foundation pays operators, not individual divers, for each starfish treated and logged correctly. For
Starfish Sweep 2026 the rates are:
Mae Haad: 45 baht per starfish. The pilot rate was 30 baht.
Sail Rock: 60 baht per starfish, to reflect the longer boat trip and stronger currents.
Fuel support for Sail Rock: 1,200 baht per day on which the operator makes at least one sweep dive
at Sail Rock. There is no fuel support for Mae Haad.
Payments are capped at 400 starfish per operator per calendar week (Monday to Sunday), across both
sites together. Starfish treated above the cap are still welcome and still counted toward the campaign
target, but they are not paid. The Foundation pays by bank transfer on or before the 10th day of the
month after the dives, based on the ReefTally records. Queries about a payment must be sent within 30
days of the transfer date.
An operator that does not log a dive in ReefTally for 21 days in a row is treated as inactive. It must return
its kits, but it may rejoin by contacting the field coordinator.
6. Funding and partners
The campaign has a total budget of 2.4 million baht. Of this, 1.5 million baht comes from a grant by the
Nok Thale Coastal Trust, 600,000 baht from the Koh Phangan Dive Operators' Circle through a voluntary
20-baht reef levy that member shops add to each guest dive, and the remaining 300,000 baht from the
Foundation's reserves. The budget covers operator payments, fuel support, injection kits, training and
two follow-up surveys, which are planned for 8–12 December 2026 and 9–13 February 2027.
"Our members see the damage on every dive at Sail Rock," said Chanchai Meesuk, Chair of the Koh
Phangan Dive Operators' Circle. "Guests have been happy to pay the levy once we explain where the
money goes."
Survey results will be published on the Foundation's website within three weeks of each survey.
Members of the public who see crown-of-thorns starfish at other sites around Koh Phangan, Koh Tao or
Koh Samui are asked to send a photo and location to the Foundation, but not to touch or try to remove
the starfish themselves.
Notes for editors
The Thale Khiao Reef Foundation is a non-profit marine conservation organisation founded in 2014 and
based in Thong Sala, Koh Phangan. It runs reef monitoring at nine sites in the western Gulf of Thailand, a
coral nursery at Mae Haad and school education visits. Field operations for Starfish Sweep 2026 are led
by Ratchada Inthawong, Field Coordinator, who handles operator registration, kit issue and payment
queries.
Media contact: Ploynapat Srisuk, Communications Officer, Thale Khiao Reef Foundation, telephone 077
349 218, email press@thalekhiao-reef.example. Photographs and underwater video from the September
survey are available on request. Interviews with Dr. Kanittha Sombatwong can be arranged on weekdays
between 10:00 and 16:00.
— Ends —

Internal Memo: New Rules for Holding Clients'
Original Documents
Lom Sak Community Legal Aid Centre, Phetchabun · Ref. LSC-MEMO-2026-08 · 14 September 2026
To: All staff lawyers, paralegals, intake volunteers and front desk staff
From: Atchara Wongkhamchan, Managing Lawyer (Room 201, ext. 201)
Subject: Central custody of original documents, receipts and returns, effective 1 October 2026
1. Background
On 22 July 2026 the original land title deed of a client in a boundary dispute could not be found for 9
days. It was found in a closed file box sent to the archive by mistake. A court hearing had to be
postponed. A review of open files in August found 61 originals held in case folders, desk drawers and
two staff vehicles. The management meeting of 9 September 2026 decided as follows.
2. Decision
From 1 October 2026, no original client document may be kept in a case folder, desk drawer, bag or
vehicle. Every original the centre accepts must be held in the fireproof document safe in the Records
Room (Room 104, ground floor) and entered in the Original Documents Custody Register kept by the
Document Custodian. Case folders and CaseNest will hold scanned copies only.
Until 30 September 2026 the responsible lawyer could keep an original in a locked desk drawer for up to
5 working days. That allowance is not replaced.
3. Which documents are covered
Land title deeds and other land rights documents, including Nor Sor 3 certificates.
House registration books, vehicle registration books and original birth or marriage certificates.
Signed contracts, loan agreements, pawn tickets, court orders and judgments.
Thai national ID cards and passports are treated differently. Staff copy them and give them back before
the client leaves the building. The only exception is when the document must be shown at court the next
morning: the case lawyer may then hold it overnight in the safe, with the written approval of the
Managing Lawyer recorded in CaseNest before 16:00 that day.
4. Receiving an original at the centre
1. Fill in receipt form LA-07 in two copies, listing each document with its number and the number of
pages. The client signs both copies and keeps one.
2. Scan every page and upload the scan to the client's file in CaseNest under the tab "Originals held".
3. Seal the documents in a numbered tamper-evident envelope marked with the case number.
4. Hand the envelope to the Document Custodian in Room 104 before 16:00 on the same day. The
custodian checks the contents and signs the register.

5. If you receive an original after 16:00, place the sealed envelope in the locked drop slot in the door of
Room 104. The custodian opens the slot at 08:30 the next working day and records it.
Note. Intake volunteers may not accept originals at all. If a client arrives with originals for a first
interview, the volunteer asks the duty lawyer to come to the front desk and complete the receipt.
5. Mobile clinics
At the Wednesday mobile clinic in Khao Kho and the monthly clinic at Nam Nao District Office, lawyers
accept copies only. If a client is unable to travel because of age, disability or illness, the lawyer may
accept up to 3 originals at the clinic. They must be sealed in the grey travel pouch on site, recorded on
form LA-07, and handed to the Document Custodian by 10:00 on the next working day.
6. Responsibilities
Document Custodian (Suwimon Thepkhamta, Room 104, ext. 104): keeps the safe keys and the
Custody Register, checks every envelope on arrival, and carries out a full count of all originals on the
last working Friday of each month.
Deputy Custodian (Wiraphon Saengdao, paralegal, ext. 108): performs all custodian duties when
Suwimon Thepkhamta is on leave or away.
Case lawyer: completes the receipt and arranges the return to the client.
Managing Lawyer: approves overnight holding of ID cards and passports, decides on unclaimed
documents, and leads the response to any loss.
7. Returning originals to clients
When a case is closed, the case lawyer contacts the client within 5 working days to arrange the return of
all originals. The client signs the return section of form LA-07. Another person may collect only with the
client's signed letter of authority and a copy of the collector's ID card. If the client does not collect within
90 days of the first contact, the centre sends a registered letter. Documents unclaimed 180 days after
closing are referred to the Managing Lawyer. The centre never destroys a client's original document.
8. Loss or damage
Any member of staff who finds that an original is missing or damaged must report it to the Managing
Lawyer within 2 hours of discovery and complete incident form LA-12 the same day. The Managing
Lawyer informs the client within 24 hours. Staff must not contact the client about it first.
9. Transition
All originals currently held outside the safe must be handed to the Document Custodian with a
completed form LA-07 by Friday 16 October 2026. The custodian and the Deputy Custodian will audit
every open file from 19 to 23 October 2026.

Domstad Veterinary Teaching Clinic, Utrecht · Clinical Engineering Section · DS-ICU-017 rev. C · Issued 14 September

1. IDENTIFICATION AND SCOPE
This data sheet describes the two AeroNest OK-90 oxygen therapy kennels installed in the small-animal intensive care
ward (room B1.07, ground floor of the Hoefslag building) of the Domstad Veterinary Teaching Clinic. The kennels are
made by Zeldenrust Medisch B.V., Amersfoort, and are registered under clinic asset numbers DVTC-ICU-0412  (left
bay) and DVTC-ICU-0413  (right bay). The smaller OK-60 cat kennel in the isolation unit (room B2.19) is covered by
sheet DS-ICU-018. Rev. C adds the CO2 flow rule (section 4) and the brachycephalic limits (section 6). Calculations
are planning aids only; the built-in oxygen analyser reading always takes precedence.
2. TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS
Internal dimensions: 90 cm wide × 65 cm deep × 70 cm high (gross volume 409.5 L). Net gas volume with the
floor mattress, drip tray and cooling duct fitted: V = 395 L.
Patient size: dogs and cats up to 40 kg body mass; maximum floor load 60 kg. Larger dogs receive nasal oxygen
(ICU protocol P-14).
Door: polycarbonate front door with two 12 cm iris ports for handling without opening the door.
Gas inlets: oxygen inlet with NIST connector, supplied at 4.0 bar from the wall outlet; flow meter range 0 to 30
L/min; second inlet for medical air; nebuliser port NB-2 .
Oxygen analyser: galvanic cell, range 0 to 100 % O2, accuracy ±2 % vol; sensor cartridge ZM-OX-31 , replace
every 18 months or when the 100 % calibration fails.
Climate module: Peltier cooling, 350 W, chamber temperature adjustable from 16 °C to 28 °C; humidity alarm
above 70 % RH.
CO2 absorber: rear canister holding 1.2 kg soda lime (granules 2 to 4 mm); bypass valve BV-1  on the canister lid.
Electrical: 230 V, 50 Hz, 3.2 A; connected to the red (emergency power) sockets only.
3. TIME TO REACH THE TARGET OXYGEN LEVEL
When the door is closed and oxygen flows in, the oxygen fraction inside the kennel rises towards the inlet value along
a wash-in curve. The time needed to reach a target fraction is estimated with equation (1).
t = VQ × ln( Fin − F0Fin − FT ) (1)
where t is the fill time (min), V the net gas volume of the kennel (395 L), Q the fresh-gas flow (L/min), Fin the oxygen fraction of
the inlet gas (0.99 for wall oxygen), F0 the starting fraction (0.21 for room air) and FT the target fraction set on the controller.
Worked example. At Q = 15 L/min from room air to a target of 40 % O2: V/Q = 395/15 = 26.3 min; ln((0.99 −
0.21)/(0.99 − 0.40)) = ln(0.78/0.59) = 0.279; t = 26.3 × 0.279 = 7.4 min. In fast-fill mode (30 L/min, allowed for the first
10 minutes only) the same kennel reaches 50 % O2 in about 6.1 min.
4. CARBON DIOXIDE CONTROL
When the soda lime canister is in use, CO2 is absorbed and the flow is chosen for oxygen only. When the canister is
bypassed (valve BV-1  on "OFF", for example during nebulisation or when the granules are exhausted), the flow itself
must wash the CO2 out. The CO2 production of the patient is first estimated from body mass with equation (2).

̇VCO2 = k × m0.75 (2)
where V̇ CO2 is the CO2 production (L/min), k the clinic's resting coefficient of 0.011 L/min per kg0.75 (use 0.016 for patients
with a body temperature above 39.5 °C) and m the body mass in kg.
The minimum fresh-gas flow that keeps the CO2 level in the kennel at or below the limit then follows from equation (3).
Qmin =

where Qmin is the minimum fresh-gas flow (L/min), xmax the permitted CO2 fraction in the kennel (0.010, i.e. 1.0 %; until rev. B
the limit was 0.5 %) and xin the CO2 fraction of the inlet gas (0 for wall oxygen, 0.0004 when medical air is mixed in).
Worked example. A 20 kg Border Collie on wall oxygen with the canister bypassed: m0.75 = 200.75 = 9.46, so V̇ CO2 =

above the result, here 11 L/min.
5. OXYGEN SUPPLY AND BACK-UP CYLINDERS
During a pipeline shut-down a back-up cylinder is connected through regulator RG-200 . The available running time of
a cylinder is estimated with equation (5).
tcyl = Vw × ( P − Pr )Q (5)
where tcyl is the running time (min), Vw the water capacity of the cylinder (10 L for the clinic's back-up cylinders), P the gauge
pressure read on the regulator (bar), Pr the reserve pressure that must stay in the cylinder (20 bar) and Q the set flow (L/min).
Worked example. A full cylinder at 200 bar with a flow of 10 L/min gives tcyl = 10 × (200 − 20)/10 = 180 min. A
cylinder below 50 bar is not connected to a kennel; it is returned to the gas store (room A0.03) with a red "EMPTY"

6. OPERATING LIMITS FOR PATIENTS
Standard target range: 40 % to 60 % O2. A setpoint above 60 % is allowed for at most 24 h and needs written
approval of the ICU clinician on duty in the patient record.
Minimum fresh-gas flow at any time: 4 L/min, even when the soda lime canister is in use and the target has been
reached.
Chamber temperature: 18 °C to 24 °C for dogs; 20 °C to 26 °C for cats.
Brachycephalic patients. For brachycephalic breeds (for example French Bulldog, Pug, English Bulldog, Persian
cat) the chamber temperature must not exceed 21 °C and the fresh-gas flow must be at least 10 L/min at all

Before each patient (ICU nurse): check the door seal, the soda lime colour and the oxygen alarm (set at 5 %

Weekly, every Monday (ICU nurse on early shift): two-point calibration of the oxygen analyser at 21 % (room air)
and 100 % (wall oxygen). Until 1 July 2026 this calibration was done monthly. Results go in the kennel logbook.
Every six months (Clinical Engineering): electrical safety and door-seal leak test.

How Long Is Slack Water Really? Usable Intervention Windows at
the Eynhallow Sound Test Berths, 2023–2025
Isla M. Flett, Magnus Rendall and Kirsty A. Linklater
Marine Operations Research Group, Eynhallow Tidal Test Centre (ETTC), Aikerness Road, Evie, Orkney KW17 2NJ, United
Kingdom
Working paper ETTC-WP-26/03 · Version 1.2 · 14 September 2026 · Supersedes version 1.1 of 2 June 2026
ABSTRACT. Every subsea task at a tidal berth has to fit inside a slack-water window. Since 2019 the
Eynhallow Tidal Test Centre has planned these tasks with a single rule of thumb: a usable window of 45
minutes at every slack, centred on the predicted turn of the tide. We test it against 1,186 slack events recorded
at six berths in 2023–2025 and 412 logged intervention attempts. The median usable window for a work-class
ROV ranged from 19 minutes (Berth E6, spring low-water slack) to 58 minutes (Berth E1, neap high-water
slack). Windows were shorter after low water than after high water and shrank further when wind blew against
the flood. We propose class-specific current thresholds, a minimum predicted window per class, and a revised
booking procedure in the SlackPlan scheduling tool, which the Centre adopted on 1 April 2026.
1. Introduction
Eynhallow Sound, between Rousay and the West Mainland of Orkney, reaches depth-averaged speeds of more
than 3.5 m/s at spring tides, which is why the Centre placed its six grid-connected test berths there. The same
currents make subsea work difficult: divers, remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and the cable vessel can only
hold position when the flow falls below a limit that depends on the type of work, and that happens only briefly
around each turn of the tide.
The planning rule used since the Centre opened, a fixed 45-minute window centred on the predicted slack,
was taken from a harbour-engineering manual written for sheltered estuaries. Developers have complained for
several years that the rule is optimistic: of the 412 intervention attempts logged between 2023 and 2025, 97
(23.5 %) were aborted, and in 61 of those the reason recorded was current. This paper measures the usable
window at each berth and tidal state and proposes a replacement for the 45-minute rule.
2. Site and data
Each berth has a bottom-mounted acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) within 60 m of the device
foundation. Records were averaged over 2-minute blocks and over the lowest 10 m of the water column, where
divers and ROVs work; gaps longer than 10 minutes removed 74 slack events, leaving 1,186. The berths, E1 to
E6, lie in a line running north-east from the Evie shore, from Berth E1 (chart depth 24 m, 0.6 km offshore) to
Berth E6 (45 m, 2.1 km offshore); peak spring currents rise from 2.4 m/s at E1 to 3.8 m/s at E6.
Wind data come from the Centre's mast at Aikerness, and significant wave height (Hs) from the wave buoy
moored 1.2 km west of Berth E6.
3. Defining a usable window
We define the usable window as the longest continuous period, around a predicted slack, during which the 2-
minute depth-averaged speed stays below the threshold for the class of work. Thresholds, agreed with the
contracted dive and ROV teams at Kirkwall in November 2025, are:
Class D (surface-supplied diving): 0.30 m/s.
Class O (observation-class ROV, inspection only): 0.50 m/s.
Class W (work-class ROV, tooling and connector work): 0.75 m/s.
Class C (cable vessel on dynamic positioning, cable lift or lay): 1.00 m/s.
Class W is the reference class for the results below because it accounts for most of the work at the site (183
of the 412 attempts). The window is measured from the moment the speed first falls below the threshold to the
PAGE 1 OF 3 EYNHALLOW TIDAL TEST CENTRE · SLACK-WATER WINDOWS · ETTC-WP-26/03

moment it first rises above it again.
4. Results
4.1 Window length by berth and tidal state
Table 1 gives the median Class W window for each berth, separated into spring and neap tides (tidal range
above or below the mean range of 2.9 m at Kirkwall) and into high-water and low-water slack. Windows
shorten steadily with distance offshore, and the low-water slack is 8 to 10 minutes shorter than the high-water
slack at every berth because the ebb starts abruptly. At Berths E4 to E6 no tidal state reached the old 45-minute
assumption.

4.2 Wind, swell and prediction error
Wind blowing against the direction of the flood (from the north-west sector, 280° to 340°) shortened the
window most. With a mean wind of 10 m/s or more from that sector, the median Class W window fell by 31 %
at Berths E4 to E6 and by 22 % at Berths E1 to E3. Wind from other sectors had no measurable effect below 14
m/s. Above Hs = 1.5 m, ROV pilots reported loss of station-keeping near the surface even when the near-bed
current was within limits. SlackPlan's harmonic predictions placed the minimum current within ±6 minutes of
the observed slack in 80 % of events; storm surge delayed the turn by up to 22 minutes. Teams who started at
the predicted slack, rather than when the profiler showed the current had dropped, lost a median of 7 minutes.

5. Revised planning rules
From the results we derived a minimum predicted window for each class: the median task length from Table 2

Head of Marine Operations must approve the split plan in writing at least 48 hours before the first slack. No equivalent
exception exists for diving.
6. Booking procedure
This procedure replaces section 3 of the Berth Client Operations Guide (issue 7). A cancelled booking may
move to another slack in the same 14-day period without repeating steps 1 to 3 if that slack also meets Table 3.
1. At least 10 working days before the planned date, the berth client enters the task in SlackPlan, giving the
berth, class of work, task length in minutes and the preferred slack (HW or LW).
2. SlackPlan returns the predicted window for that class for each slack in a 14-day period; the client selects a
slack whose predicted window meets the minimum in Table 3.
3. The client uploads the method statement and the dive or ROV team's competence records; the booking is
then sent to the approver named in Table 3.
4. At 16:00 on the day before the work, the Marine Operations Desk checks the wind and wave forecast
against Table 3, applies the 30 % wind reduction if needed, and confirms or cancels the booking by e-mail.
5. On the day, the team may put a diver or vehicle in the water only when the live reading from the berth's
ADCP has been below the class threshold for 4 consecutive minutes, not at the predicted slack time.
6. The team leader reports the end of the task, or an abort and its reason, to the Desk on VHF channel 73
within 15 minutes of recovery.

Carbon Dioxide in Brewery Cellars: Ventilation and Alarms
Ing. Radka Šimáčková (Safety and Process Training) and Ing. Petr Kalous (Head Cellar Master)
Training Centre, Pivovar Doudlevce a.s., Na Celné 41, 301 00 Plzeň, Czech Republic
Lecture notes for the Cellar Air Safety course SKL-2 · Module 3 of 4 · Rev. 4 · issued 8 September 2026
ABSTRACT. These notes accompany the three-hour Module 3 lecture of the Cellar Air Safety course SKL-2,
which every employee and contractor working below ground level at Pivovar Doudlevce must complete. They
explain how to estimate the carbon dioxide (CO2) released by our vats and tanks, how to check the ventilation,
how long a room stays safe if the fans stop, and how to respond to a Sensilo CD-40 alarm. Rev. 4 replaces Rev.
3 (March 2025). The calculations are planning aids and never override a monitor reading.
1. Scope of these notes
The rules in this module apply to the four below-ground areas of the Doudlevce site: the open fermentation hall
F1 (level −1, 1,150 m3, kept at 8 °C), the sandstone lagering cellars L1 to L6 (level −2, kept at 1–3 °C), the
bright beer room B2 (level −1, 640 m3, kept at 12 °C) and the yeast propagation room Y1 (level −1, 210 m3).
Module 3 is taught on the first Tuesday of each month in training room 014 next to the cellar entry desk,
from 07:30 to 10:30, and ends with a 20-question written test (pass mark 16 of 20). A refresher is required
every 24 months; staff whose refresher is overdue by more than 30 days lose their cellar access badge until they
attend.
2. Why carbon dioxide is the main cellar hazard
Fresh outdoor air contains about 0.04 % CO2 by volume. Carbon dioxide is odourless and about 1.5 times as
dense as air, so it collects in floor channels, sumps and the stair wells to level −2. For this reason all fixed
sensors are mounted 30 cm above the floor, not at breathing height.
For training purposes the brewery uses the following reference levels (site rules, not medical advice):
0.5 % (5,000 ppm): highest 8-hour shift average; ventilation design target.
1.5 % (15,000 ppm): highest short exposure, 15 minutes at most.
3 % (30,000 ppm): headaches, poor judgement.
Above 8 %: loss of consciousness within minutes.
3. Estimating how much CO2 a cellar releases
During fermentation, yeast converts sugar into ethanol and CO2. In the open vats of hall F1 practically all of
this gas escapes into the room; in the lagering tanks the spunding valves vent the excess into the cellar. The
laboratory measures the apparent extract of every vessel twice a day, so the extract drop is used to estimate the
gas release. The mass of CO2 released in a period is
m = k × V × ΔE (1)
where m is the mass of CO2 released (kg), k the release coefficient, fixed at 0.42 kg of CO2 per hectolitre per
degree Plato for all Doudlevce lager worts, V the volume of beer in the vessels concerned (hl) and ΔE the drop in
apparent extract over the period (°P).
The hourly gas release rate converts this mass to a volume with the density of CO2:
g = mρ × h (2)
where g is the CO2 release rate (m3/h), m the mass from formula (1) (kg), ρ the density of CO2 at the room
temperature (kg/m3) and h the length of the period over which ΔE was measured (hours, normally 24).
PAGE 1 OF 3 PIVOVAR DOUDLEVCE · SKL-2 MODULE 3: CO2 IN CELLARS · REV. 4

Use these density values: 1.96 kg/m3 for the lagering cellars L1–L6 (0–4 °C), 1.91 kg/m3 for hall F1 and room
Y1 (5–10 °C) and 1.88 kg/m3 for the bright beer room B2 (11–16 °C). Rev. 3 used a single value of 1.98 kg/m3
for every room; calculations made with it before 8 September 2026 slightly underestimate the gas volume and
must be redone at the next ventilation review.
Example 1 (hall F1 at peak fermentation). On day 3 of a brew, six open vats of 45 hl each (V = 270 hl)
show an extract drop of 2.6 °P in 24 hours. Formula (1) gives m = 0.42 × 270 × 2.6 = 294.84 kg of CO2 per
day. With ρ = 1.91 kg/m3 and h = 24, formula (2) gives g = 294.84 / (1.91 × 24) = 6.43 m3 of CO2 per hour.
Example 2 (lagering cellar L4). Cellar L4 holds twelve horizontal tanks of 150 hl (V = 1,800 hl). During
the first week of lagering the extract drops by about 0.15 °P per 24 hours. Then m = 0.42 × 1,800 × 0.15 =
113.4 kg per day and, with ρ = 1.96 kg/m3, g = 113.4 / (1.96 × 24) = 2.41 m3/h.
4. Is the ventilation sufficient?
If a room is ventilated with outdoor air at a constant flow, its CO2 concentration settles at a level where the gas
removed by the fans equals the gas released by the beer. Rearranging this balance and adding the site safety
factor gives the minimum fresh-air flow:
Qmin = S × gclim − cout (3)
where Qmin is the minimum fresh-air flow (m3/h), S the safety factor (1.5 for all cellar rooms; it covers uneven
mixing near the floor), g the CO2 release rate from formula (2) (m3/h), clim the design concentration of 0.005
(0.5 % by volume) and cout the outdoor concentration, taken as 0.0004 (0.04 %). Enter concentrations as volume
fractions.
Example 3 (hall F1). With g = 6.43 m3/h from Example 1, Qmin = 1.5 × 6.43 / (0.005 − 0.0004) = 1.5 × 6.43
/ 0.0046 ≈ 2,097 m3/h. Hall F1 has two extract fans, VF-1 and VF-2, each rated at 1,400 m3/h at floor level.
Both fans together (2,800 m3/h) are sufficient at peak fermentation; one fan alone is not. If either fan is out of
service, no more than four vats may be at days 2 to 4 of fermentation at the same time.
For cellar L4, Example 2 gives Qmin = 1.5 × 2.41 / 0.0046 ≈ 786 m3/h, well within the 1,200 m3/h of the
shared level −2 fan VL-3. The installed fan capacities of the other rooms are: B2, 900 m3/h (fan VB-1); Y1, 450
m3/h (fan VY-1); L1–L3 together, 1,600 m3/h (fan VL-1); L5 and L6 together, 1,000 m3/h (fan VL-4).
5. How long a room stays safe if the fans stop
When the ventilation stops, the CO2 released by the beer stays in the room and the concentration rises. Ignoring
leakage through doors and stair wells (which makes the answer conservative), the time until a given
concentration is reached is
t = Vroom × ( cA − c0 )g (4)
where t is the time after the fans stop (hours), Vroom the free air volume of the room (m3), cA the concentration
of interest as a volume fraction (for example 0.015 for the main alarm), c0 the concentration when the fans
stopped (volume fraction, read from the monitor) and g the CO2 release rate (m3/h).
PAGE 2 OF 3 PIVOVAR DOUDLEVCE · SKL-2 MODULE 3: CO2 IN CELLARS · REV. 4

Example 4 (hall F1, fan power cut). The monitor reads 0.10 % (c0 = 0.001) when both F1 fans stop at peak
fermentation (g = 6.43 m3/h). The main alarm level of 1.5 % is reached after t = 1,150 × (0.015 − 0.001) /
6.43 ≈ 2.5 hours, and the pre-alarm level of 0.5 % after 1,150 × (0.005 − 0.001) / 6.43 ≈ 0.72 hours, i.e. about
43 minutes.
The free air volumes used for formula (4) are: F1, 1,150 m3; B2, 640 m3; Y1, 210 m3; L1, 780 m3; L2, 760
m3; L3, 740 m3; L4, 820 m3; L5, 690 m3; and L6, 610 m3. These volumes exclude tanks and vats (survey of
May 2026).
6. The Sensilo CD-40 monitoring system
Every below-ground room has at least two fixed Sensilo CD-40 infrared CO2 sensors (hall F1 has four), all
mounted 30 cm above the floor and wired to the panel at the cellar entry desk on level 0. The thresholds are:
Pre-alarm at 0.5 % (5,000 ppm): yellow lamp, intermittent tone. Until 31 August 2026 the pre-alarm was
set at 1.0 %; all sensors were reprogrammed to 0.5 % in the first week of September 2026.
Main alarm at 1.5 % (15,000 ppm): red beacon, continuous siren, fans switch to boost mode
automatically.
Evacuation alarm at 3.0 % (30,000 ppm): red beacon and two-tone siren in all rooms on the same level;
access doors unlock for exit and lock for entry.
Each fixed sensor receives a bump test with 2.0 % test gas every 30 days by the night shift electrician and a
full two-point calibration every 6 months by the service contractor. A sensor that fails a bump test is marked
with a red tag; until it is replaced, the room may only be entered with a portable monitor and a second person
waiting at the door.
7. What to do when an alarm sounds
The response depends on the alarm level. On a pre-alarm, safely stop the task within five minutes, check the
fans and report the reading to the shift leader by radio. On a main alarm or an evacuation alarm, follow these
steps in order:
1. Stop work immediately.
2. Leave the room by the nearest exit, keeping your head as high as possible; never go down into a lower
area, a sump or the level −2 stair well to leave.
3. Report to the assembly point at the cellar entry desk on level 0 and give your name to the desk attendant,
who checks it against the entry log.
4. Do not re-enter to rescue a colleague. Call the site emergency number 4444 and tell the attendant who is
missing and where they were last seen. Only the trained rescue team with breathing apparatus may go in.
5. Re-entry is allowed only after the shift leader has confirmed with a portable monitor, from the doorway,
that the reading is below 0.5 % and the fans have run in boost mode for at least 20 minutes.
Fan bypass. No one may switch a cellar fan off or put a sensor in maintenance mode while staff are in the room. Bypassing
the fan interlock for maintenance requires a written permit signed by the Head Cellar Master (Ing. Petr Kalous) or, in his
absence, the duty process engineer, and is limited to one shift.

PRESS RELEASE · REF. TS-IMP-2026/09 · PORTO ALEGRE, 22 SEPTEMBER 2026 · FOR IMMEDIATE PUBLICATION
Tinturaria Sarandi turns spent wattle bark into Casca
Viva, a natural-dye service for small fashion labels
Tinturaria Sarandi Ltda. · Avenida Assis Brasil 9120, Sarandi, Porto Alegre – RS · Press office
From 5 October 2026 the Porto Alegre dye works will take orders for six brown, grey and graphite
shades dyed with tannin-rich black-wattle bark that a tannin extraction plant in Montenegro used to
burn as boiler fuel.
What is being launched
Tinturaria Sarandi Ltda., a commission dye house
founded in 1961, today announced Casca Viva, a line
of piece-dyed shades obtained from the spent bark of
the black wattle tree (acácia-negra). After partial tannin
extraction for the leather industry, the residue still gives
fast, warm colours on cotton, linen and wool with an
alum or iron mordant.
Casca Viva is aimed at independent labels and ateliers
that cannot meet the 1,000 kg minimum of the
company's conventional reactive-dye service. The pilot
lot minimum is 25 kg of fabric per shade. The preview
shown at a Porto Alegre design fair in June 2026
quoted a 50 kg minimum; that figure has been
withdrawn. First production batches are scheduled for
19 October 2026.
"For sixty years we have dyed with synthetic colour and
treated the effluent afterwards. Casca Viva starts from a
residue that already exists sixty kilometres up the road
and needs no salt at all," said managing director
Rosângela Wiederkehr, granddaughter of the founders
Heinrich and Olga Wiederkehr.
Where the bark comes from
The bark is supplied under a five-year agreement
signed on 2 September 2026 with Extratos Vale do Caí
Ltda., a tannin extraction plant in Montenegro, about
60 km from the dye works. The agreement covers up to
1,150 tonnes of spent bark per year, dry basis. It is
delivered twice a week and stored in a new 600 m2
shed beside the dye house.

How the process works
The bark is extracted at 95 °C in a new 3,000-litre
autoclave and the liquor is pumped to two 250 kg low-
liquor-ratio jet machines. Fabric is mordanted in the
same machine, so a batch takes about five hours
instead of the eight to nine of a reactive-dye cycle.
Exhausted bark is pressed and burnt in the plant's own
biomass boiler.
"Natural colour is never as uniform as a reactive dye,
and we say so openly. Every bulk lot is measured
against the approved lab dip and leaves with a printed
lot card," said technical director Everton Bortolini.

VARMI · CUSTOMER NEWSLETTER NO. 31 · OCTOBER 2026
Melting the driveway with water you have already paid
for
Laugarvirki hf. · Geothermal district heating for Reykjavík, Kópavogur, Garðabær and Mosfellsbær · Ref. VAR-2026-31 ·
Published 1 October 2026
Before the first frost, our network team explains how to size a snow-melt loop on your house's return
water, when you need a sealed top-up valve, and what the new cold-alert rule means for your steps and
driveway this winter.
A second life for warm water
Every cubic metre of hot water that reaches a
Laugarvirki customer arrives at about 76 °C and leaves
the radiators at roughly 30 °C. Because you pay by
volume at the main meter, the heat still left in that
return water costs you nothing extra. Running it
through plastic pipes under a driveway, path or front
steps before it goes to the drain is the cheapest way to
keep paving free of ice in the capital area, and around
41,000 of our 68,500 connected properties already do
it.
The catch is that return water alone is often too cool, or
there is too little of it, on the coldest mornings. Many
homeowners then add a top-up valve that mixes in
fresh supply water. That water is metered and billed,
and on cold-alert days it competes with radiators
across the city. This feature shows how to work out
whether you need one.
One household's numbers
Halldóra Sveinsdóttir and Einar Bragason live in a 1987
terraced house on Logafold in Grafarvogur. Their 48 m2
driveway and 10 m2 path stayed icy along the north
edge every January, and the six concrete steps to the
door (6 m2) were the worst of all. Their plumber
measured a winter return flow of 0.40 m3/h at 31 °C.
"We assumed we needed a bigger loop," says
Halldóra. "In fact the loop was fine; there just wasn't
enough warm water going through it." The worked
example below uses their figures.
Design melt rates
Network engineer Þórdís Kjartansdóttir sets the
planning values in our Snow-Melt Connection Guide,
edition 4 (May 2026):
Residential driveways, paths and parking spaces:
220 W/m2 (the 2019 edition used 250 W/m2).
Steps, ramps and landings: 320 W/m2, because
water runs off and wind exposure is higher.
Commercial forecourts and loading bays: 380
W/m2.
Design outlet temperature of the loop: 10 °C; never
plan below 5 °C, as the pipe surface may then
freeze.
P = qdAd + qsAs (1)
where P is the design melting power of the area (W), qd the melt rate for driveways, paths and parking (220 W/m2), Ad
their area (m2), qs the melt rate for steps, ramps and landings (320 W/m2) and As their area (m2). Divide by 1,000 for kW.
Pr = k · Fr · ( Tr − To ) (2)
where Pr is the heat available from the return water (kW), k = 1.15 kWh per m3 per °C the heat content of geothermal
water used in all our guides, Fr the winter return flow of the house (m3/h), Tr the return temperature entering the loop (°C)
and To the loop outlet temperature (°C, normally 10 °C).
LAUGARVIRKI HF. · VARMI NO. 31 · SNOW MELTING WITH RETURN WATER · VAR-2026-31 PAGE 1 OF 2

Ft = P − Prk · ( Ts − To ) (3)
where Ft is the top-up flow of fresh supply water needed (m3/h), P the design power from (1) in kW, Pr the return-water
heat from (2), and Ts the supply temperature: 76 °C in supply zones A to G, 71 °C in zone H (Úlfarsárdalur and
Norðlingaholt). If P is not larger than Pr, no top-up is needed.
C = p · Ft · H (4)
where C is the extra hot-water cost for one winter (ISK), p the volume price (ISK 167 per m3 from 1 September 2026; ISK
158 until 31 August 2026), Ft the top-up flow from (3) and H the hours per winter the top-up valve is open (we plan with
350 h for the capital area, 420 h for Mosfellsbær above 100 m).
Worked example: Logafold
1. Design power, equation (1): 58 m2 × 220 W/m2 + 6
m2 × 320 W/m2 = 12,760 + 1,920 = 14,680 W, i.e.
14.68 kW.
2. Return-water heat, equation (2): 1.15 × 0.40 × (31 −
10) = 9.66 kW. The deficit is 14.68 − 9.66 = 5.02
kW.
3. Top-up flow, equation (3), zone C: 5.02 / (1.15 × (76
− 10)) = 0.0661 m3/h, about 66 litres per hour.
4. Winter cost, equation (4): 0.0661 × 350 h = 23.1 m3,
and 23.1 × 167 = about ISK 3,870 a winter (ISK
3,660 at the old price).
The family's top-up valve was sealed at 66 L/h in March
2026. Einar notes that the steps now clear before the
school run.
Registering a top-up valve
A top-up valve may only be fitted and opened after
Laugarvirki has registered and sealed it. The order is:
1. Your master plumber, licensed in Iceland, sends
form SB-2 through the Mínar síður customer portal
with the calculation above and a sketch of the loop.
2. We review the form within 10 working days and
reply with a valve size and flow limit.
3. The plumber fits a thermostatic limiter set to no
more than 45 °C at the loop inlet, and a separate
top-up meter which we supply (rental ISK 38 per
day, billed with your heating account).
4. A Laugarvirki inspector visits, checks the limiter and
puts a numbered lead seal on the valve. Only then
may it be opened.
The registration fee is ISK 14,900. Breaking a seal, or
running an unregistered top-up, is charged ISK 45,000
per occasion under section 9 of our General Terms of
Supply, and we may remove the valve.
Cold-alert days
When the forecast for Reykjavík is −8 °C or colder for
two or more consecutive days, we declare a Kuldavakt
(cold alert) by text message and on our website at least
12 hours in advance. During a Kuldavakt, every sealed
top-up valve must be closed from 06:00 to 11:00 and
from 17:00 to 20:00, so that radiators get the full
supply pressure at peak times.
The rule covers top-up water only. A loop that runs
purely on the house's own return water may stay on
around the clock, because it takes no extra water from
the network. The one exception for top-up valves is a
ramp or step registered as an accessible entrance (form
SB-4) at a care home, health clinic or the home of a
registered wheelchair user: these may stay open during
peak hours, limited to the ramp or steps only.
Last winter we called four Kuldavakt periods totalling
11 days; on 17 January 2026 peak demand reached
2,140 litres per second.
Before you dig. Loops must be pressure-tested at 6 bar for two hours before paving, and the return line must
still pass through the main meter's return side. Our sizing check is free.

and swarm calls are handled by Calum Imrie, Apiary Liaison Officer.
Application window 1 November 2026 to 15 January 2027 (17:00)
Decision letters sent by 28 February 2027
Move-in window 20 March to 10 April 2027
Colonies removed by 15 October 2027
2. WHO MAY APPLY
Applicants must be at least 18 years old, live within 25 km of the garden, and have kept bees for
at least two full seasons. Applicants with only one season of experience may apply if they name a
mentor who holds a permit in the same season and who agrees in writing to supervise inspections.
Each applicant may hold one permit and place colonies on one stand only.
Public liability insurance covering beekeeping with a minimum cover of £5 million per claim.
Until the 2026 season the minimum was £2 million; certificates at the old level are no longer
accepted.
A colony health certificate signed by a qualified bee health inspector, dated no more than 30
days before the colonies arrive.
3. HIVE STANDS AND COLONY CAPACITY
The number of colonies a stand can take depends on the flowering area that bees from the stand
can use. Forage inside the garden counts in full; open green space outside the walls within 1 km
(Blackford Hill, the Hermitage of Braid) counts at 30 % because it is shared with other apiaries.
The capacity of each stand is set with equation (1).
Hmax = ⌊ As + 0.3 × Ana ⌋ (1)
where Hmax is the maximum number of colonies on the stand, As the flowering area inside the garden
assigned to the stand (ha), An the green space outside the walls within 1 km of the stand (ha), a the
forage area required per colony, set at 0.9 ha from the 2027 season (it was 1.2 ha until 2026), and ⌊  ⌋
means rounding down to a whole colony.
Worked example, Stand B (Orchard Bank): As = 2.3 ha and An = 5.0 ha. The weighted area is
2.3 + 0.3 × 5.0 = 3.8 ha; 3.8 / 0.9 = 4.22, rounded down to 4 colonies.
Capacities for the 2027 season:
Stand A, Rock Garden Terrace: As 1.6 ha, An 3.5 ha, capacity 2 colonies.
Stand B, Orchard Bank: As 2.3 ha, An 5.0 ha, capacity 4 colonies.

Stand C, Heath Garden North: As 1.1 ha, An 8.2 ha, capacity 3 colonies.
Stand D, Nursery Yard: As 0.8 ha, An 2.0 ha, capacity 1 colony; reserved for applicants with
one season of experience and their mentors.
No stand may hold more than 6 colonies in any case, and nucleus colonies of five frames or fewer
count as half a colony.
4. CALCULATING THE PERMIT FEE
The permit fee is made up of a non-refundable application fee and a colony charge for each month
a colony is on site. Any part of a calendar month counts as a full month. The fee is calculated with
equation (2).
F = F0 + c × h × m × ( 1 − δ ) (2)
where F is the total permit fee (£), F0 the application fee of £60 (it was £45 for the 2026 season), c the
colony charge of £4.80 per colony per month, h the number of full colonies on the permit, m the
number of months on site, and δ the discount rate: 0.25 for Trust volunteers who logged at least 40
volunteer hours between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026, 0.50 for students enrolled on the
Trust's Certificate in Garden Beekeeping, and 0 for everyone else. The discount applies to the colony
charge only, and the two discounts cannot be combined; the higher one is used.
Worked example: a beekeeper with no discount keeps 2 colonies on Stand C from 20 April to 30
September 2027, which is 6 months (April to September). F = 60 + 4.80 × 2 × 6 × (1 − 0) = 60
+ 57.60 = £117.60.
The colony charge is invoiced with the decision letter and must be paid within 14 days, otherwise
the offer lapses.
5. SITING DISTANCE FROM PUBLIC PATHS
Hives on a stand must be set back from the nearest path open to the public. The minimum
distance is set with equation (3).
dmin = 3 + 1.2 × hs (3)
where dmin is the minimum distance in metres between the front of the nearest hive and the edge of
the nearest public path, and hs the total number of colonies on the stand from all permit holders
together (a nucleus counts as 0.5).
Worked example: Stand B with 4 colonies needs dmin = 3 + 1.2 × 4 = 7.8 m.
Screen exception. Where a solid fence, wall or dense hedge at least 2.0 m high stands between
the hives and the path along the whole stand, the distance from equation (3) is halved. The
halved distance may never be less than 3.0 m. Stands A and C have qualifying walls; Stands B
and D do not.
6. COLONY HEALTH AND DISEASE RULES
All colonies must be inspected by the permit holder at least every 10 days from the start of May to
the end of July, and at least every 21 days at other times of the season. Varroa mite levels must
be monitored once a month using a sticky board or an alcohol wash, and logged.
Colonies may not be brought on site if they come from an apiary within 5 km of a confirmed case
of American or European foulbrood in the previous 12 months, unless the colonies have had two
clear inspections by a qualified bee health inspector at least 6 weeks apart, the second one no
more than 30 days before arrival. Suspected foulbrood or any other notifiable pest found on site

must be reported to the Apiary Liaison Officer the same day; the Trust will then close the stand to
all colony moves until it is cleared in writing by an inspector.
Syrup feeders must be inside the hive; open feeding is not allowed.
7. WORKING ON SITE
Permit holders may enter the garden through the service gate on Cluny Lane between 07:00 and
09:30, and after 17:30 until dusk, using the key fob issued with the permit. Hive inspections are
not allowed while the garden is open to visitors, except for swarm control on Stand D.
When a swarm is reported, the permit holder must arrive within 2 hours; otherwise a £35 call-out
charge is added to the next invoice.
8. HONEY AND THE TRUST'S SHARE
Honey belongs to the permit holder, but the Trust keeps a share of the surplus above a basic yield
per colony. The Trust's share is set with equation (4) and is due by 31 October 2027.
S = 0.12 × max ( 0, Y − 9 × h ) (4)
where S is the Trust's share of honey (kg), Y the total weight of honey extracted from the permit
holder's colonies in the season (kg), h the number of colonies on the permit, and 9 kg the basic yield
per colony that the permit holder keeps in full.
Worked example: 3 colonies yield Y = 58 kg in total. The surplus is 58 − 27 = 31 kg, so S =
0.12 × 31 = 3.72 kg. It may be paid in cash at £14 per kg instead (here £52.08). A permit holder
whose total yield is 9 kg per colony or less owes nothing.
9. SELECTION, BREACHES AND WITHDRAWAL
If a stand receives more requests than its capacity, places are offered in this order: first, holders of
a 2026 permit with no recorded breach; second, Trust volunteers who qualify for the 0.25
discount; third, all other applicants, by a ballot held on 3 February 2027 in the Garden Office.
A breach is any of: missing a required inspection interval twice; two missed swarm calls; open
feeding; an inspection while the garden is open (other than on Stand D); or failing to report
suspected foulbrood the same day. One breach leads to a written warning. A second breach in the
same season ends the permit, and colonies must be removed within 7 days.
Withdrawal and refunds. A permit holder who removes colonies voluntarily and tells the Apiary
Liaison Officer in writing before 1 July 2027 receives a refund of the colony charge for each full
month remaining. No refund is given for removals notified on or after 1 July 2027, or when a
permit ends because of breaches. Where the Trust closes a stand for disease, the colony charge for
the months the stand is closed is refunded in full, whatever the date. The application fee is never
refunded.
